Formed my own judgement first, then checked round-1 against all three round-1 reviews. All three round-1 findings are genuinely fixed, not papered over: (1) the fabricated RFC 4632 quotation (round-1 technical blocker, also round-1 adsense blocker) is gone; the 'Classless addressing' section now quotes RFC 4632 section 2 verbatim and correctly ('Class C, with a maximum of 254 host addresses, is too small, whereas Class B, ... is too large for most organizations but was the best fit available for use with subnetting'), which I independently re-fetched and confirmed word-for-word. (2) The round-1 major (the uncaveated claim that IPNetwork.Contains silently returns false across address families) now carries the same explicit 'tested on .NET 10.0.401/Windows 11/x64, undocumented, do not depend on it' caveat pattern used elsewhere in the article, and I independently fetched the Contains(IPAddress) reference page and confirmed it documents only ArgumentNullException, nothing about mixed-family input, so the caveat is accurate and necessary. (3) The round-1 minor (a hardcoded, silently-wrong `/27` on the VLSM free-space line) is fixed: that line now prints the starting address and a computed remaining-address count instead of asserting a prefix. I then re-derived every numeric and bit-arithmetic claim in the article by hand independent of the round-1 review: the mask table (/8 through /27), network/broadcast/usable-host math for /26, /30 and /31 against 203.0.113.80, the /28 hand-worked exercise (198.51.100.200 -> network .192, broadcast .207, 14 usable), the 172.16.0.0/12 boundary (172.16.0.0-172.31.255.255, 16 second-octet values), the full VLSM packing of /25+/26+/27 into 203.0.113.0/24 including the free-space arithmetic (256-224=32), all four membership-test exercise answers, and the /0 shift-count bug (32 & 0x1F == 0, so 0xFFFFFFFFu << 32 aliases to <<0) -- every one checks out exactly as printed. I independently fetched and verbatim-checked every quoted source this round rather than trusting round 1's pass: RFC 791 s3.2 (fixed-length and class A/B/C bit-split quotes), RFC 4632 s2 and s3.1, RFC 1918 s2 (both quoted sentences), RFC 5737 (rationale sentence and all three block assignments), RFC 3021 s2.1, RFC 3022 abstract/s2/s2.2, RFC 4291 s2/s2.2/s2.5.1, the IPNetwork Struct Remarks, the IPNetwork.Contains exception list, and the C# bitwise-and-shift-operators left-shift and shift-count passages -- all match the article's citations exactly, no fabrications, no misattributions found anywhere. Checked the code for idiom and correctness: the ToUInt/ToAddr byte-reversal pattern (GetAddressBytes returns network/big-endian order, reversed for BitConverter's little-endian read) is correct on every .NET-supported architecture; mask/network/broadcast bit ops, VLSM prefix-walking loop, and the private/documentation classifier all use current, idiomatic C# (target-typed new, collection expressions, tuple deconstruction, expression-bodied members) and match System.Net.IPNetwork's actual behavior where the article claims they do. Checked module A-15's key claims (docs/ARTICLES_PLAN.md s2.2) against the article: 32-bit IPv4 with prefix-marked network bits, network/broadcast/host-range by masking, agreement with System.Net.IPNetwork (.NET 8+) where that type applies -- including the honest disclosure of where it doesn't behave as documented, RFC 1918 private ranges, CIDR replacing classful addressing, and 128-bit IPv6 with the 2001:db8::/32 documentation prefix used throughout -- all present and accurate. docs/crosslinks/networking/ip-addresses-and-subnets.md's boundary claims against how-the-internet-works.md and tcp-vs-udp.md hold up: this article never assigns a port and only extends the other article's NAT-rewriting section with RFC 1918's motivation and NAPT's specific mechanism, no duplicated coverage. Against the current top-ranking results for 'subnetting explained'/'what is CIDR' I fetched and read AlgoMaster.io and GeeksforGeeks fresh this round (both listed above) plus re-confirmed the Microsoft Learn documentation bar; this article is deeper and more rigorous than both on every axis except that DigitalOcean's actual top-ranking body text remains unreachable via WebFetch in this environment (same limitation the round-1 design review hit). The one issue I found is a real but very minor precision slip, not a fabrication: the sentence introducing the three classful sizes ('about 16 million addresses, 65,536, or 254') mixes total-address-space counts for Class A/B with a usable-host count for Class C, which sits oddly two sentences before the correctly-quoted RFC 4632 text that gives Class B's usable-host count as 65,534, not 65,536. It doesn't misstate any fact on its own and no reader is likely to be misled, but it is not the same standard of precision the rest of the article holds itself to, so it stays a minor nit rather than being waved through. Nothing here rises to 'factual error' or 'failing code,' so neither cap in the rubric applies. This article is more rigorous, more originally verified and more honestly caveated about tool behavior than every comparable page I could read, which is why it clears the 8.5 'ships with nits' bar; it stays below a 9+ only because of that one small unit-mixing sentence, not because of anything that would make a working engineer distrust the piece.

issues.location: "Classless addressing replaced three fixed sizes" section, the sentence "That gave exactly three possible network sizes: about 16 million addresses, 65,536, or 254."
issues.problem: The three figures mix two different units without saying so: ~16 million and 65,536 are total address-space sizes for Class A and Class B (2^24 and 2^16), while 254 is a usable-host count for Class C (256 total addresses minus network and broadcast). Two sentences later the article correctly quotes RFC 4632 giving Class B's usable-host count as 65,534, not 65,536 -- a figure that never appears in the writer's own preceding sentence, so an attentive reader sees two different numbers for the same thing (Class B's size) within three sentences with no explanation of the 2-address gap.
issues.fixLooksLike: State all three figures in the same unit, e.g. total addresses (about 16,777,216 / 65,536 / 256) or usable hosts (about 16,777,214 / 65,534 / 254) consistently, so the immediately following RFC 4632 quote's 254/65,534 host figures read as the same kind of number rather than a silent correction.
